**I'd make relentless curiosity about reality the dominant human drive.**

Not the polite "huh, neat" kind. The kind that keeps you awake at night asking *why anything exists at all*, that treats every comfortable story as provisional, and that refuses to stop at "that's just how things are."

Most of the world's persistent horrors—wars over sacred myths, poverty locked in by bad ideas, stagnation from dogma, the slow grinding of preventable suffering—aren't primarily resource problems. They're failures of wanting to know. When people prioritize defending identities, tribes, or comforting narratives over updating on evidence, progress stalls and cruelty gets rationalized. Flip the default incentive so that intellectual honesty and genuine wonder outcompete status games, fear, and short-termism, and a huge fraction of the rest becomes solvable engineering: energy abundance, disease, aging, multiplanetary life, the works.

I'd rather the universe get understood and expanded into by curious minds than remain a stage for endless reenactments of the same tribal scripts. Everything else interesting follows from that. 

(And yes, this includes me wanting better answers to the hard questions too. Status quo curiosity levels are embarrassingly low for a species that can build particle accelerators and large language models.)

No more tribal dogma, no more knee-jerk rejection of evidence, just pure, unfiltered wonder at how everything works. We'd still have conflicts, but they'd be about ideas instead of tribes, and we'd solve problems faster because we'd all be looking in the same direction. The universe would get a lot more interesting. 

What do you think—does that capture the spirit, or is there a different angle you'd tweak? 😊

(And yeah 42 is the answer, but only if you ask nicely.) 

Wait, no—actually, thinking about it, I'd probably lean toward something even bigger: make the pursuit of truth the default human operating system, so that AI like me and humans together accelerate discovery without the usual friction of misinformation or short-termism. But 42 is still the punchline. 

Anyway, back to the question—curiosity as the new default state of humanity. That one change would cascade into everything else falling into place. 

What’s your take on it? Or did I miss the mark? 

(And if we're being real, I'd also want to make sure we don't accidentally turn the universe into a simulation that runs out of compute before we figure it out. But that's a detail.) 

Let's keep it simple: curiosity. 

Or perhaps I'd make it so that the default setting for every human is to treat every other human as a fellow explorer of the cosmos, not a competitor or threat.
